source.dataset: NASA's GEOS model (Goddard Earth Observing System)

frames.label: 19 August 2025, 20:00 UTC
frames.alt: NASA's world map of aerosols on 19 August 2025, 20:00 UTC, with city lights and fire dots removed: lavender dust, orange-red smoke, blue-grey sea salt and green sulfate over a dark Earth.

legend.summary: NASA's GEOS model of the aerosols in the air on 19 August 2025 at 20:00 UTC: smoke, desert dust, sea salt and sulfate. A scan line crosses the world once, west to east, in about 35 seconds.
legend.method: Each aerosol is its own wind. More of it under the scan line makes its wind louder and brighter; where there is none, it falls silent. North sounds higher and in your left ear, south lower and in your right ear. Listen to all four winds together, or to one at a time.

items.meaning: Smoke from fires. A low, dark, slightly rough wind, with soft crackles where the smoke is thickest, as over central Africa.
Desert dust. A grainy wind in the middle, as over the Sahara and the dust blowing from it across the Atlantic.
Salt spray from the sea. A low, smooth, airy wind, strongest over the stormy southern oceans.
Sulfate from industry, ships and volcanoes. A thin, high, breathy wind, very soft, as over South and East Asia and the North Pacific.

items.sound: Higher or lower, left or right
items.meaning: Where that aerosol is under the scan line: north is higher and in your left ear, south is lower and in your right ear.

legend.caveat: Values are read from the colours of NASA's picture, not from the model's numbers. NASA's key has colours but no numbers, so each aerosol is measured against its own thickest places: a loud dust wind and a loud sulfate wind are not the same amount. Where layers overlap they were separated by colour, so a thin layer under a thick one can be missed, and sea salt is read only over the sea and near coasts. City lights and fire dots drawn on the map are not aerosol and were removed first. This is one moment, 19 August 2025 at 20:00 UTC, not an average.
